newsitem.title: USA: Alcoa CEO seeks probe into LME aluminum.
newsitem.headline: Alcoa CEO seeks probe into LME aluminum.

text.p: Alcoa, the world's biggest aluminum producer, is to ask the London Metal Exchange (LME) and the producer group IPAI to look for ways to avoid manipulation in the aluminum market, the company's chairman and CEO Paul O'Neill said.
O'Neill told Reuters in a telephone interview he was concerned over how 10,000 tonnes of aluminum was placed on warrant in a Rotterdam LME warehouse last Friday.

O'Neill said trader Barclays Metals was rumored to be the company which took the big chunk of off-warrant, or non LME registered metal and placed it on warrant, thereby causing Friday's LME stock report to show a sharp hike.
This was the first increase of any size for some time in stocks when fundamentals were good, he said.
Barclays, which is a ring dealing member of the LME, said it had no comment on Alcoa's remarks.

"I gives me some pause when I see this situation where apparently somebody, rumored to be Barclays, and I am not saying they did it, attempted to influence the price of the world market by a paper transaction," O'Neill said.
"They did not like the direction the metal price was taking and so they dumped the 10,000 tonnes onto warrants in an attempt to influence the price going down," O'Neill said.
"If we as producers had done the same kind of trick the regulators would have been all over us for attempted manipulation of the market," O'Neill said.
"It's not quite reasonable for the regulators and the anti-trust officials to simply look the other way when financial interests are trying to manipulate the market," O'Neill said.
"Therefore it does seem to me there ought to be some inquiry by the London Metal Exchange," O'Neill said. "We have already had the Sumitomo affair."
A more through way of collecting facts about physical metal in the market would reduce the room for any manipulation, O'Neill said.

Although LME from October 1 will report stocks of all metals in warehouses, on or off warrant, O'Neill said this may not be enough because any speculator could remove the metal a few blocks to somebody else's property.

"I plan to write a letter to the LME and the IPAI (International Primary Aluminium Institute) suggesting they give some consideration to some way to get all the facts out in the open place so that manipulation is not a concern or consideration in world commerce of this kind," O'Neill said.
LME inventories were shrinking day by day, O'Neill said, but the price of aluminum was going down, in defiance of basic textbook economics.
"That suggests something, perhaps including intentional manipulation," O'Neill said.

A broker for an LME ring dealing member, who declined to be quoted publicly, said it was a well known that metal was being stored off warrant, but it would be difficult to get everyone to report how much unregistered stocks they owned.
"I don't see why the movement of 10,000 tonnes from one place to another could be seen as manipulation," the broker said. "It's a bit futile to try to make everything transparent."
Aluminum producers were one of the main beneficiaries of aluminum stocks being financed by banks and other institutions, the broker said.

Meanwhile O'Neill said Alcoa had no intention of restarting its idled capacity because the market did not need the extra aluminum, suggesting that LME stocks would have to fall to at least below 500,000 tonnes.
LME stocks totaled 656,925 tonnes on Thursday.
